title: Domain Adaptive Transfer Learning with Specialist Models

numbers.sentence: Each image can have multiple labels and on average, each image has 1.26 labels.

While this is less than half of the full ImageNet dataset of 1.2 million examples, the transfer learning results are slightly better than using the full ImageNet dataset for many of the target datasets.
We observe an absolute gain of about 0.6% in accuracy, achieving results comparable to Cui despite using less pre-training data.
For Inception v3 models, we pre-train from random initialization for 2,000,000 steps using Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with Nesterov momentum.
We used a learning rate schedule that first starts with a linear ramp up for 20,000 steps, followed by cosine decay.
AmoebaNet-B models followed a similar setup with pre-training from random initialization for 250,000 steps using SGD and Nesterov momentum.
We used larger mini-batches of 2,048 examples to speed up training.
Models were trained for 20,000 steps using SGD with momentum.
We used a similar learning rate schedule with a linear ramp for 2,000 steps, followed by cosine decay.
We have seen an increase in dataset sizes since ImageNet; for example, the YFCC100M dataset has 100M examples.

tables.caption: dataset statistics. We hand-picked several subsets by hand-selecting labels based on the target dataset. We compare our methods against these hand-picked subsets.

tables.name: Table 3
tables.caption: Transfer learning results with Inception v3. Each row corresponds to a pre-training method. Adaptive transfer refers to our proposed method described in section . Each column corresponds to one target dataset. Results reported are top-1 accuracy for all datasets except Oxford-IIIT Pets, where we report mean accuracy per class. All our results are averaged over 5 fine-tuning runs. Adaptive transfer is better or competitive with the hand selected subsets.
tables.label: table:transfer_results

tables.name: Table 4
tables.caption: Transfer learning results with AmoebaNet-B. Each row corresponds ot a pre-training method. Adaptive transfer refers to our proposed method. Results reported are top-1 accuracy for all datasets except Oxford-IIIT Pets, where we report mean accuracy per class. All our results are averaged over 5 fine-tuning runs. Huang also use the AmoebaNet-B model, but with a larger input image size at , while we used image inputs instead.
tables.label: table:transfer_results_amoebanet

tables.name: Table 5
tables.caption: Transfer learning performance on Oxford Flowers 102 with Inception v3. We report the mean per class accuracy, averaged over 5 runs. The first two rows are our results, showing that adaptive transfer improves over training over the entire ImageNet dataset. Our method performs as well as Cui despite using less pre-training data.
tables.label: table:compare_data_selection_method

tables.name: Table 6
tables.caption: Transfer performance on Oxford-IIIT Pets from subsets of the same size (80M), using the top 4k selected labels, but with different weighting schemes: Adaptive Transfer Weights are the weights from our method, Uniform is a uniform distribution on all selected labels, and Reverse is a distribution obtained by swapping the weights between the highest and the lowest weighted labels from the Adaptive Transfer distribution.
tables.label: table:transfer_perf_different_distribution
